newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC summit hands Clinton free trade victory.
newsitem.headline: APEC summit hands Clinton free trade victory.

text.p: Asia-Pacific leaders handed U.S. President Bill Clinton a victory on liberalising trade in information technology at a summit in the Philippines on Monday.

Support by leaders of 18 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) economies was qualified for a U.S. plan to scrap tariffs on trade in computers, memory chips and telcommunications equipment worth an annual $500 billion.
But Clinton hailed it as "big deal" that would boost U.S. exports and create higher-paying jobs.

The fourth APEC summit in Subic Bay, a former U.S. naval base north of Manila, passed a Manila Action Plan to create the world's largest free trade zone embracing two billion people and more than half of global economic output.
APEC calls for developed countries to free all trade by 2010 and developing nations by 2020.

"I came out optimistic," Australian Prime Minister John Howard said after APEC leaders agreed on concrete steps to forge a single Pacific Rim trading bloc. "Not deliriously optimistic because you have to be pragmatic."
Clinton managed to slot the information technology agreement into a summit declaration, snatching the deal during a informal pre-summit dinner on Sunday after APEC ministers came up with a fudge.
Washington was pressing for zero tariffs on information technology by a 2000 deadline.

The declaration called on the World Trade Organisation to "substantially eliminate tariffs by the year 2000" in its first ministerial meeting in Singapore next month. But it "recognised the need for flexibility".
U.S. officials put the best possible interpretation on the agreement. "Substantially eliminate is tradespeak for zero," said U.S. Trade Representative spokesman Jay Ziegler.
Asian leaders laid more stress on the escape clauses.

"If we are not ready we will not have to submit to the deadline," said Malaysian Prime Minister Mohamad Mahathir. The text, he said, "gives us some leeway, some flexibility on the actual date of implementation".

Chinese President Jiang Zemin said: "Because of the differences in the levels of economic development in the member economies, it is very difficult for the liberalisation in the field to be pushed forward in accordance with a timetable".
China is not a member of the WTO, and in his meeting with Jiang on Saturday Clinton made clear it would not get U.S. support for entry until it did more to open its markets.
However, on Monday Chinese foreign minister Qian Qichen said Beijing expected to conclude negotiations with the United States over accession in the first half of next year.

Jiang said Beijing would cut import duties to an average 15 percent by 2000 after reducing them to an average 23 percent this year. "China will continue to support the 'APEC approach'," the Chinese Xinhua news agency quoted him as saying.

The information technology accord was Clinton's second breakthrough at this year's summit. On Sunday he agreed with Chinese President Jiang Zemin to swap visits to each other's capitals and end an almost decade-long chill.
"Every year we sell $100 billion in information technology and that sector supports almost two million jobs in the United States," Clinton said after the one-day summit.
"So imagine if we went to zero tariffs in the entire world. That would mean to America more exports and higher paying jobs," he told U.S. embassy employees.

In other business, APEC heads agreed to accept Vietnam and Peru as new members by 1998, earlier than previously expected, according to Mahathir. APEC's three-year moratorium on new admissions expired this year.

Protesters who headed for Subic Bay in a motorcade of 500 gaily-decorated jeepneys -- minibus copies of World War Two U.S. jeeps -- denounced the forum's goal of liberalising trade on grounds it would negatively affect poorer countries.

Organisers halted the caravan more than halfway north along the road from Manila to Subic, saying confrontation with heavily armed riot police would be suicide. Earlier terrorist threats to the summit failed to materialise.

On the lawn of the clifftop summit site in a former U.S. officer's club overlooking Subic Bay, Philippine President Fidel Ramos read the declaration calling for "substantial, concrete, measurable and sustainable results" for APEC.
Earlier, some of the region's most powerful business executives met to forge deals and contacts and act as a "reality check" on APEC.
The Manila Action Plan focused a raft of market-opening measures offered by individual APEC members to ease flows of trade and investment and business travel.
